screens.title: Load Balancing with Nginx and HAProxy
screens.narratorSegment: In large web deployments a single server quickly becomes a bottleneck. Load balancing presents one stable endpoint to clients while distributing work across multiple backend servers to improve availability and responsiveness. In this chapter you will see two widely used software options: Nginx, which doubles as a reverse proxy and basic balancer using upstream groups, and HAProxy, a specialist load balancer with powerful health checks and monitoring. You will learn how to configure Nginx upstream blocks and balancing algorithms, and how to install, configure, and monitor HAProxy including health checks and the statistics page. Along the way we’ll cover common pitfalls — session persistence, misconfigured health checks, and single points of failure — and practical patterns to avoid them. By the end you’ll be prepared to set up a simple HAProxy front end for multiple Flask backends, validate health checks, and use the stats page to troubleshoot. Think of this chapter as the practical bridge between single-server apps and a highly available front line for production traffic. What part of your architecture would improve first with a load balancer?

screens.title: What is load balancing?
screens.narratorSegment: Load balancing is the process of distributing incoming network traffic across multiple backend servers so that work is shared, response times stay low, and availability remains high when individual servers fail. The balancer presents a single access point to clients while managing which backend receives each request. A helpful analogy is a restaurant host seating arriving parties: the host keeps the dining room even, avoids overload at any single table, and redirects parties to another waiter or table if a section is unavailable. In system terms, the load balancer monitors backend availability and forwards client requests only to healthy servers. One common misconception is that load balancing alone solves scale forever; it does not. You still need capacity planning, caching, and horizontally scalable application components. Another confusion is thinking the balancer always preserves client affinity; that depends on algorithm choices like ip_hash or source. A concrete example: a web site uses three application servers behind a balancer; if one app server crashes, the balancer detects failure and stops forwarding requests to it, keeping the site available. Takeaway: load balancing centralizes traffic control, but it must be combined with monitoring and correct configuration to provide real resilience. How would you test that a balancer correctly removes a bad backend?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Load balancing distributes requests across multiple servers, providing availability and responsiveness while masking backend changes from clients.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is load balancing?
Distribute traffic across many servers to improve availability and performance.
Definition & role

A load balancer receives client requests and forwards them to a pool of backend servers. It tracks health, enforces balancing policies, and hides failures from clients.

Everyday analogy

Think of the load balancer as a restaurant host: it seats guests to spread load, and it redirects guests if a server or table is unavailable.

Common misconceptions
  • Load balancing is not a substitute for capacity planning.
  • Session persistence requires explicit algorithm choices or shared sessions.
Concrete example
A web app has three identical servers. The balancer uses round‑robin so repeated requests rotate among them. If one server fails, it stops receiving traffic until healthy.
Why it matters

Without a balancer, a single overloaded server creates slow responses and downtime. With a balancer, traffic shifts and availability improves.

Key Takeaway

A load balancer centralizes traffic routing, but resilience depends on health checks, monitoring, and proper algorithm choice.

screens.title: Configure Nginx as a load balancer
screens.narratorSegment: Nginx can act as a reliable software load balancer using an upstream block to define backend servers and proxy_pass to forward requests. The upstream group names backends and accepts optional parameters like weight, and directives to switch algorithms such as least_conn or ip_hash. In the server section you use proxy_pass to reference the upstream group, and set headers to preserve client information. A typical minimal configuration defines an upstream with three servers and a server block that proxies traffic to that group. A concrete example is running three app instances on port 8080. If you add weight=3 to one server, Nginx will favor it by sending more requests there. A misconception is assuming ip_hash guarantees perfect session persistence for all clients; it ties persistence to client IP, which can change for mobile users or NATed clients. Another common error is forgetting proxy_set_header lines, which can break host-aware applications. When you test, watch the backend logs or responses to confirm the distribution you expect. Takeaway: Nginx is ideal for simple balancing and session affinity via ip_hash, but choose HAProxy when you need richer health checks or advanced routing.

keyIdea.title: Nginx load balancing
keyIdea.text: Use upstream blocks and proxy_pass to send requests to backend groups; set headers and choose algorithms appropriate to your session needs.

content.html:
Nginx Configuration
Configure Nginx as a load balancer
Define upstream groups and forward requests with proxy_pass.
Config example
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/loadbalancer.conf
upstream backend_servers {
  server backend1.example.com:8080;
  server backend2.example.com:8080;
  server backend3.example.com:8080;
  # least_conn; # optional: least connections
  # ip_hash;    # optional: session affinity
}

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name myapp.example.com;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://backend_servers;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
  }
}
Explanation bullets
  • The upstream block names a server pool referenced by proxy_pass.
  • By default Nginx uses round‑robin; enable least_conn or ip_hash for other behaviors.
  • proxy_set_header preserves client address and Host so backends can log and respond correctly.
Concrete scenario
Three app servers on port 8080 behind Nginx. Add weight if one server has more capacity.
Key Takeaway

Nginx is excellent for straightforward HTTP load balancing. Use ip_hash for simple affinity, but test for NAT or mobile clients.

screens.title: Balancing algorithms and when to use them
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right load balancing algorithm changes how traffic is distributed and affects session behavior and latency. Round‑robin cycles through backends sequentially and works well when servers are similar and requests are short. Least‑connection sends new requests to the server with the fewest active connections, which helps when requests have variable durations. ip_hash in Nginx or source in HAProxy derives a backend from the client IP, providing simple session persistence without shared session storage. A common misconception is to use ip_hash universally for sessions; it can break when many clients share an IP due to NAT or when a client's IP changes frequently. Another pitfall is using round‑robin for long‑running connections, which can overload a server. Concrete example: for long-polling APIs choose least‑conn; for stateless web assets choose round‑robin; for an app relying on local server sessions choose ip_hash/source. Test by observing backend logs and connection counts when exercising each algorithm. The takeaway is to match the algorithm to workload characteristics and session requirements, and always validate behavior under realistic traffic. Balancing algorithms and when to use them means match algorithm to workload: round‑robin for uniform requests, least‑conn for variable durations, ip_hash/source for simple affinity.. In practical terms, round‑robin, least‑conn, and ip_hash/source compared. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Algorithm guidance
keyIdea.text: Match algorithm to workload: round‑robin for uniform requests, least‑conn for variable durations, ip_hash/source for simple affinity.

content.html:
Comparison
Balancing algorithms and when to use them
Tradeoffs for distribution, persistence, and variable workloads.
Round‑robin
Cycles through servers evenly. Good for uniform, stateless requests.
When to use
Static assets, short requests, similar server capacity.
Least‑conn
Sends new requests to the backend with fewest active connections. Helps for long-lived or uneven requests.
When to use
APIs with long processing, WebSocket or long-polling connections.
ip_hash / source
Maps client IP to a server for session persistence without shared session storage.
When to use
Legacy apps that store sessions locally and lack shared session stores.
Concrete example
A shopping site using client cookies but not shared sessions can use source to keep a shopper on the same backend. If shoppers use mobile networks with carrier NAT, validate that many clients don’t collapse to the same backend.
Key Takeaway

Select an algorithm based on session needs and request characteristics; test under realistic traffic.

screens.title: HAProxy architecture and configuration sections
screens.narratorSegment: HAProxy is a specialized load balancer and reverse proxy designed for high performance. Its configuration is organized into sections with clear responsibilities. The global section holds system-wide settings such as logging, chroot, and user privileges. Defaults provide behavior inherited by frontend and backend sections, like timeouts and logging options. The frontend section defines how HAProxy listens for incoming client connections and which backend to use as default_backend. The backend section lists the servers that handle proxied requests and contains balancing algorithms and health check options. There is also a listen section, typically used for the stats page where frontend and backend behavior is combined into a single block. A common misunderstanding is that HAProxy magically auto-detects backends; you must declare each server and the health check rules explicitly. Concrete example: a frontend bound to port 80 forwards to web_backends, which lists three servers and uses option httpchk for health checks. The key operational insight is that HAProxy separates connection handling (frontends) from pool membership and health logic (backends), enabling very fine-grained control over routing and checks. HAProxy architecture and configuration sections means global and defaults set system and default behavior; frontend handles incoming connections; backend defines servers and health logic; listen can expose stats.. In practical terms, global, defaults, frontend, backend, and listen explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
HAProxy Overview
HAProxy architecture and configuration sections
global
System-level settings: logging, user, chroot, maxconn, and sockets for stats.
defaults
Timeouts, retries, logging mode, and options inherited by frontends and backends.
listen
Combined frontend/backend used commonly for a stats interface.
frontend
Defines how HAProxy accepts client connections (bind directives) and which backend to use.
backend
Lists servers, balancing algorithm, and health check parameters like option httpchk and server check flags.
Key Takeaway

HAProxy separates listening from backend logic so you can tune health checks and balancing independently of connection handling.

screens.title: A basic HAProxy configuration for HTTP
screens.narratorSegment: This example shows a practical HAProxy configuration for HTTP load balancing. The global block sets logging and maxconn. Defaults establish mode, timeouts, and common options. A frontend binds to port 80 and forwards to a backend called web_backends. In the backend we set balance roundrobin and enable an HTTP health check with option httpchk GET /health. Each server line includes check parameters controlling the check interval and the criteria to mark a server up or down. For example, setting inter 2000 makes HAProxy check every two seconds; rise 2 requires two consecutive successful checks to mark a server up, and fall 3 marks it down after three failures. One common mistake is forgetting to test the configuration with the check command before reloading; always validate syntax with haproxy -c -f to avoid taking the service down. Another error is leaving the stats page unsecured. The concrete result: after reload, HAProxy will route traffic to healthy backends and show server status on the stats page. Try toggling a backend to see it appear as DOWN in the UI and watch traffic shift away.

keyIdea.title: HAProxy snippet
keyIdea.text: Use global and defaults for system settings, frontend to accept traffic, and backend with option httpchk and server checks to manage pool health.

content.html:
HAProxy Example
A basic HAProxy configuration for HTTP
global
    log /dev/log local0
    user haproxy
    group haproxy
    maxconn 20000

defaults
    mode http
    timeout connect 10s
    timeout client 1m
    timeout server 1m

frontend http_frontend
    bind *:80
    default_backend web_backends

backend web_backends
    balance roundrobin
    option httpchk GET /health
    server web1 192.168.1.101:8080 check inter 2000 rise 2 fall 3
    server web2 192.168.1.102:8080 check inter 2000 rise 2 fall 3
    server web3 192.168.1.103:8080 check inter 2000 rise 2 fall 3 backup
Line-by-line highlights
  • maxconn limits global connections to protect the host.
  • defaults set HTTP timeouts and logging to avoid repetition.
  • option httpchk instructs HAProxy to use an HTTP GET for health verification.
  • server ... check inter 2000 rise 2 fall 3 configures frequent checks and up/down thresholds.
Practical tip
Always run sudo haproxy -c -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg before reloading to validate syntax and checks.
Key Takeaway

Configured checks and sensible timeouts make HAProxy resilient to transient backend failures and reduce false positives.

screens.title: Health checks and server state management
screens.narratorSegment: Health checks are a central responsibility of a load balancer. HAProxy can perform active HTTP checks such as GET /health and decide server state based on the responses. Key parameters control the behavior: inter sets the interval between checks, rise defines how many consecutive successes mark the server UP, and fall defines how many failures mark it DOWN. For example, with inter 5000 and fall 3, HAProxy will mark a server down after three failed checks, which takes 15 seconds. Health checks avoid sending traffic to broken servers, but a poorly chosen endpoint or timeout can create false negatives. A common mistake is checking a non‑representative path that returns 200 even when the service is degraded. Use a lightweight, accurate health endpoint that verifies the parts of the stack your frontend requires. Another useful pattern is to set backup servers that only receive traffic when primary servers are down. Concrete example: configure option httpchk GET /health and observe the stats page while stopping a backend; you should see it transition to DOWN after the configured failures. Takeaway: tune inter, rise, and fall for your environment to balance detection speed and noise.

keyIdea.title: Health check tuning
keyIdea.text: Set inter, rise, and fall to balance prompt failure detection against transient network blips; pick meaningful health endpoints.

content.html:
Health Checks
Health checks and server state management
How checks work
  1. HAProxy issues a check at the interval defined by inter.
  2. Successful checks count toward rise; failures count toward fall.
  3. After rise successes the server is marked UP; after fall failures it is marked DOWN.
Example calculation
inter 5000 and fall 3 → 3 × 5s = 15 seconds to mark DOWN after consecutive failures.
Best practices
  • Use a lightweight health endpoint that verifies real readiness.
  • Set reasonable timeouts so transient network delays don’t cause false DOWN states.
  • Consider separate readiness and liveness checks for complex apps.
Concrete scenario
If a new deployment causes the health endpoint to return 500, HAProxy will mark that server down after the configured fall count and stop sending it traffic.
Key Takeaway

Health checks must be accurate and tuned. Wrong endpoints or aggressive thresholds can create instability instead of resilience.

screens.title: Monitoring HAProxy and troubleshooting backends
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring gives you the evidence you need to operate a balancer. HAProxy includes a stats page you can enable in a listen section, which shows backend server status, session counts, and response rates. It is invaluable for spotting a server marked DOWN, identifying high connection counts, and confirming failover behavior. Logs are also critical: HAProxy writes HTTP and connection logs to the system log when configured, and these show rejects, retries, and backend errors. A common troubleshooting path is: reproduce the error, check the HAProxy stats page for server health, inspect backend logs to find the root cause, and verify network connectivity and firewall rules. One mistake is leaving the stats page open to the public; always protect it with basic auth and firewall rules. For example, enable listen stats on port 8080 with stats auth and then use the UI to see the web_backends pool and test stopping a backend to validate that traffic moves away. Takeaway: the stats page and logs together provide a fast feedback loop for diagnosing backend reachability and health check misconfigurations. Monitoring HAProxy and troubleshooting backends means use the haproxy stats ui and logs to observe server state and ensure the stats interface is secured.. Monitoring & Stats
Monitoring HAProxy and troubleshooting backends
Stats page
Expose a listen block on a non‑public port, enable stats uri and auth, and use it to observe backend UP/DOWN, sessions, and errors.
Example listen snippet
listen stats
  bind *:8080
  mode http
  stats enable
  stats uri /haproxy?stats
  stats auth admin:password123
Troubleshooting steps
  1. Reproduce the issue from a client.
  2. Check HAProxy stats for backend health and connection counts.
  3. Inspect backend logs and firewall rules for reachability problems.
  4. Validate health check endpoints return appropriate status codes.

Protect the stats page with authentication and restrict access with firewall rules to trusted IPs.

screens.title: Deployment considerations and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: When deploying a balancer, several operational considerations matter. First, ensure network reachability: the load balancer must be able to reach backend server ports and clients must reach the balancer. Firewalls on the balancer and backends often block traffic by default; open the necessary ports. On RHEL systems SELinux can prevent HAProxy from connecting to arbitrary ports; you may need to set the haproxy_connect_any boolean or configure port contexts. Second, a single load balancer is itself a potential single point of failure. For true high availability, deploy two load balancers and use a virtual IP with Keepalived to failover or use active‑active approaches. Third, logging and monitoring: enable comprehensive logging on both HAProxy and backends and integrate logs with your monitoring stack. Common mistakes include incorrect health checks that cause premature marking of servers as DOWN and not protecting the stats page. A practical example: if SELinux blocks HAProxy connections, the balancer appears to drop connections even though configs are correct. The takeaway is to validate network, SELinux, and firewall settings before concluding a configuration is wrong. Which operational check will you automate first?

content.html:
Deployment
Deployment considerations and common mistakes
Network reachability
Open ports on load balancer (e.g., 80, 8080 for stats) and allow backend ports (e.g., 5000 or 8080) from the balancer host.
SELinux
On RHEL setsebool -P haproxy_connect_any=1 if HAProxy cannot connect to backend ports, or adjust port contexts appropriately.
High availability
Use two load balancers with Keepalived and a virtual IP for active/passive failover, or active‑active clusters for higher throughput.
Logging & monitoring
Enable HAProxy logging and integrate with your monitoring tools to detect patterns, not just single failures.
Common Mistakes

Misconfigured health checks, blocked firewall rules, and SELinux are common causes of perceived balancer failure. Check these first.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: HAProxy with Flask backends
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through building the lab: one HAProxy VM and two Flask backend VMs. On each backend, install Python and Flask, create an app that responds on port 5000 and exposes /health returning 200. Start each Flask app and ensure firewalls permit port 5000 from the HAProxy host. On the HAProxy host install the package for your distribution, enable and start the service, then edit /etc/haproxy/haproxy. cfg to declare a frontend on port 80 and a backend pool pointing to both backends on port 5000. Then visit the stats page and observe UP/DOWN status. As a test, stop one Flask app and watch HAProxy mark it DOWN, with traffic directed to the healthy server. This exercise verifies installation, checks, and monitoring in a production-like sequence.

keyIdea.title: Lab steps
keyIdea.text: Provision HAProxy and two Flask backends, enable health checks, validate config, and observe failover on the stats page.

content.html:
Hands-on Lab
HAProxy with Flask backends
Backend steps (each VM)
  1. Install Python and Flask.
  2. Create app.py with / and /health endpoints that reply on port 5000.
  3. Run Flask on host 0.0.0.0:5000 and allow firewall from HAProxy.
Flask snippet
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)
SERVER_NAME = "Backend 1"
@app.route('/')
def hello():
  return f"Hello from {SERVER_NAME}!
"
@app.route('/health')
def health_check():
  return "OK", 200
if __name__ == '__main__':
  app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000)
HAProxy steps
  1. Install HAProxy and enable the service.
  2. Edit /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg: add frontend on :80 and backend with servers on port 5000.
  3. Add option httpchk GET /health and a listen stats on :8080 with auth.
  4. Validate with sudo haproxy -c -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg and reload the service.
Key Takeaway

Follow the lab steps to validate health checks and stats-driven troubleshooting; stopping a backend should show it as DOWN and route traffic to healthy instances.

screens.title: Nginx or HAProxy: choosing the right tool
screens.narratorSegment: Both Nginx and HAProxy can act as load balancers, but they serve slightly different roles. Nginx is primarily a web server and reverse proxy that offers basic, reliable load balancing using upstream groups, useful when you already use Nginx for SSL termination or static assets. HAProxy is a purpose-built load balancer with very granular control over health checks, routing, and high connection throughput. Use Nginx when you want a combined web server and balancer with simpler configuration and session affinity via ip_hash. Choose HAProxy when you need advanced health checks, detailed statistics, or the highest throughput for TCP and HTTP with complex backend rules. A misconception is thinking they are mutually exclusive; many architectures use both: HAProxy as the high-performance front line with Nginx behind for TLS offload or caching. Concrete example: for a high-traffic A P I that needs strict per-backend health validation and large connection counts, HAProxy is usually the better fit. For a small website serving static content and a few app servers, Nginx often suffices. Final question to reflect on: which concerns—advanced health checks or integrated web serving—matter more for your deployment?

Comparison
Nginx or HAProxy: choosing the right tool
Nginx
Great as a web server and reverse proxy with basic upstream balancing and ip_hash support for affinity.
Best when
You need static content serving, SSL/TLS termination, and simple load distribution in one process.
HAProxy
A dedicated load balancer with advanced health checks, robust stats, and high connection handling.
Best when
You need detailed monitoring, precise health checks, or maximum throughput for TCP/HTTP workloads.

Many real systems combine both: HAProxy for front-line balancing and Nginx for TLS offload and caching behind it.

In large web deployments a single server quickly becomes a bottleneck. Load balancing presents one stable endpoint to clients while distributing work across multiple backend servers to improve availability and responsiveness. In this chapter you will see two widely used software options: Nginx, which doubles as a reverse proxy and basic balancer using upstream groups, and HAProxy, a specialist load balancer with powerful health checks and monitoring. You will learn how to configure Nginx upstream blocks and balancing algorithms, and how to install, configure, and monitor HAProxy including health checks and the statistics page. Along the way we’ll cover common pitfalls — session persistence, misconfigured health checks, and single points of failure — and practical patterns to avoid them. By the end you’ll be prepared to set up a simple HAProxy front end for multiple Flask backends, validate health checks, and use the stats page to troubleshoot. Think of this chapter as the practical bridge between single-server apps and a highly available front line for production traffic. What part of your architecture would improve first with a load balancer?

These learning objectives map directly to practical capabilities you need for resilient web services. First, you will be able to explain why load balancing matters and identify the benefits it brings, like higher availability and improved response times, using real deployment examples. Second, you will configure Nginx as a software load balancer: you will author an upstream block and use proxy_pass to forward client requests to a backend group. Third, you will install and configure HAProxy and use its configuration sections—global, defaults, frontend, backend—to route traffic and enable health checks. Fourth, you will implement and select load balancing algorithms—round‑robin, least‑conn, and ip_hash/source—and understand when to use each. Each objective is a step toward making production systems resilient. As you practice, verify competency by deploying a simple HAProxy front end and confirming backends are balanced and health‑checked. These skills reduce downtime and make troubleshooting more predictable. Which objective will you practice first in the lab?

Learning these objectives is best done in stages. Start by learning key concepts: what a load balancer is, what a backend or upstream server is, and why health checks matter. Next, understand configuration: read Nginx upstream blocks and HAProxy sections so you can predict how traffic flows. Then apply the knowledge by writing configurations and installing HAProxy with a working stats page. Finally, master the setup by testing health checks, simulating failures, and choosing the correct balancing algorithm for session behavior. For example, if your app relies on user sessions stored locally on a server, you will use source or ip_hash to keep a client tied to a server; if your app is stateless, round‑robin or least‑conn may be better. As you practice, use the milestones to verify competency: a successful HAProxy reload with valid health checks and a stats page is proof you can operate a production balancer. Which step will you run in your lab next?

Load balancing is the process of distributing incoming network traffic across multiple backend servers so that work is shared, response times stay low, and availability remains high when individual servers fail. The balancer presents a single access point to clients while managing which backend receives each request. A helpful analogy is a restaurant host seating arriving parties: the host keeps the dining room even, avoids overload at any single table, and redirects parties to another waiter or table if a section is unavailable. In system terms, the load balancer monitors backend availability and forwards client requests only to healthy servers. One common misconception is that load balancing alone solves scale forever; it does not. You still need capacity planning, caching, and horizontally scalable application components. Another confusion is thinking the balancer always preserves client affinity; that depends on algorithm choices like ip_hash or source. A concrete example: a web site uses three application servers behind a balancer; if one app server crashes, the balancer detects failure and stops forwarding requests to it, keeping the site available. Takeaway: load balancing centralizes traffic control, but it must be combined with monitoring and correct configuration to provide real resilience. How would you test that a balancer correctly removes a bad backend?

Nginx can act as a reliable software load balancer using an upstream block to define backend servers and proxy_pass to forward requests. The upstream group names backends and accepts optional parameters like weight, and directives to switch algorithms such as least_conn or ip_hash. In the server section you use proxy_pass to reference the upstream group, and set headers to preserve client information. A typical minimal configuration defines an upstream with three servers and a server block that proxies traffic to that group. A concrete example is running three app instances on port 8080. If you add weight=3 to one server, Nginx will favor it by sending more requests there. A misconception is assuming ip_hash guarantees perfect session persistence for all clients; it ties persistence to client IP, which can change for mobile users or NATed clients. Another common error is forgetting proxy_set_header lines, which can break host-aware applications. When you test, watch the backend logs or responses to confirm the distribution you expect. Takeaway: Nginx is ideal for simple balancing and session affinity via ip_hash, but choose HAProxy when you need richer health checks or advanced routing.

Choosing the right load balancing algorithm changes how traffic is distributed and affects session behavior and latency. Round‑robin cycles through backends sequentially and works well when servers are similar and requests are short. Least‑connection sends new requests to the server with the fewest active connections, which helps when requests have variable durations. ip_hash in Nginx or source in HAProxy derives a backend from the client IP, providing simple session persistence without shared session storage. A common misconception is to use ip_hash universally for sessions; it can break when many clients share an IP due to NAT or when a client's IP changes frequently. Another pitfall is using round‑robin for long‑running connections, which can overload a server. Concrete example: for long-polling APIs choose least‑conn; for stateless web assets choose round‑robin; for an app relying on local server sessions choose ip_hash/source. Test by observing backend logs and connection counts when exercising each algorithm. The takeaway is to match the algorithm to workload characteristics and session requirements, and always validate behavior under realistic traffic. Balancing algorithms and when to use them means match algorithm to workload: round‑robin for uniform requests, least‑conn for variable durations, ip_hash/source for simple affinity.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

HAProxy is a specialized load balancer and reverse proxy designed for high performance. Its configuration is organized into sections with clear responsibilities. The global section holds system-wide settings such as logging, chroot, and user privileges. Defaults provide behavior inherited by frontend and backend sections, like timeouts and logging options. The frontend section defines how HAProxy listens for incoming client connections and which backend to use as default_backend. The backend section lists the servers that handle proxied requests and contains balancing algorithms and health check options. There is also a listen section, typically used for the stats page where frontend and backend behavior is combined into a single block. A common misunderstanding is that HAProxy magically auto-detects backends; you must declare each server and the health check rules explicitly. Concrete example: in the lab, stopping a Flask backend should cause HAProxy to mark it DOWN after the configured interval, which you can confirm via the stats page. Misconfigurations in SELinux or firewall rules commonly cause symptoms that look like ugly balancer bugs, so verify those layers early. Takeaway: combine thorough testing, monitoring, and redundancy to make load balancing effective in production.
